purpose: Hidden AGI watch aims to be a fire alarm for hidden AI. The alarm level is set by these published, versioned criteria, not by our probability judgments. It goes up the day a trigger is met, comes down slowly, and every change is public and reviewed.

levels.name: Normal
levels.meaning: No level's rule is met: fewer than two Watch triggers, and nothing higher.

levels.name: Watch
levels.meaning: The conditions that would let advanced AI be hidden are present. There's no sign that it is.

levels.name: Warning
levels.meaning: Specific evidence that a hidden capability jump may exist.

levels.name: Alarm
levels.meaning: Proof beyond reasonable doubt, under the Level-3 standard, that a hidden system meets our bar or is acting. It doesn't wait for official confirmation.

evidenceStandard: A trigger counts only with a primary source (a lab, an evaluator such as METR or an AI Security Institute, a government, or a court or SEC filing) or two independent credible outlets. A single anonymous or unverified claim is logged as unverified and can never trip Warning or Alarm on its own. Level 3 needs more: the Level-3 proof standard.
rules: It goes up at once: a level rises the day its rule is satisfied. Level 3 is the exception: it is set only when a case passes the tribunal under the Level-3 proof standard.

It comes down slowly: a level drops only after its rule has gone unsatisfied for 30 consecutive days (for Watch, fewer than two W triggers met on each of those days; for Warning and Alarm, none of their triggers met). It then drops to the level the rules give that day, which can be more than one step down. A day on which the rule is satisfied again restarts the count.
Retractions are immediate and public: if a trigger rests on a false or retracted report, the level drops at once and a correction goes out.

Every level change is loud: a breaking alert is drafted the same day and sent once a person approves it, and the site banner and the alarm history, with the evidence, update at once. The daily and weekly issues are never held back: they go out on schedule and show the new level.
Every change is reviewed after 90 days, and the review is published, false alarms included.
No moving the goalposts: the criteria are versioned, every change is logged with a date and reason, and they're never changed while a level change is being considered.
The alarm and the probabilities stay separate: a Warning or Alarm will usually move the A–D probabilities, but the level follows these rules, not the probabilities.

Level 3 needs proof, not confirmation: at least three independent lines of evidence from different modalities that share no original source, every fact in them authenticated, no single innocent explanation that accounts for all the lines (each one examined in writing), and a unanimous adversarial tribunal. Official confirmation isn't required, so the alarm can fire before the secret is out. Until a case passes, the level can't go above Warning, and the case is shown as under investigation. The case is published in a format fixed in advance.

Borderline doesn't count: a trigger that compares a measured value with its threshold (a gap, a median, a share or a rate) counts only when the value comes from a measurement, a primary statement or a count from sourced records (not our judgment) and clears the threshold by more than the source's stated uncertainty. If no uncertainty is stated, it must clear it by 10%, or be confirmed by a second reading or a second lab. Until then it is shown as borderline and not counted. Date clocks and time windows are exact, so they have no borderline.

proofStandard.name: Level-3 proof standard
proofStandard.summary: Convergent circumstantial proof: beyond reasonable doubt, without needing a confession. Official confirmation is not required. If a developer confirms, the secret is already out, so the alarm has to be able to fire before that; if confirmation comes later, the alarm fired early, as intended.

requirements.title: At least three independent lines of evidence
requirements.text: At least three lines of evidence, each from a different modality, that share no original source: three reports that trace back to one leak are one line.

requirements.title: Every fact authenticated
requirements.text: Every fact in every line is authenticated and sourced to the evidence standard. The facts must be verified; the conclusion may be inferred, and the inference is argued explicitly, for example with likelihood ratios.

requirements.title: No innocent explanation covers all the lines
requirements.text: No single line needs to be conclusive, but no single innocent explanation (an investment bubble, a normal pre-release lag, misattribution, coincidence, hype, or any other) may account for all the lines together. Each one is examined in writing, showing which evidence it fails to explain.

requirements.title: A unanimous adversarial tribunal
requirements.text: The case survives an adversarial review: independent prosecution and defense investigations (the defense's job is to build the most coherent innocent story), an authenticity check on every document and quote, and a panel of independent judges who must agree unanimously that no coherent innocent explanation survives.

modalities: A compute or financial anomaly with no matching release
Capability leakage: results or artifacts that no public model can produce
proofStandard.tribunal: The tribunal is run by separate, independent instances of this site's AI agent: prosecution, defense, the authenticity check and each judge. A person approves the breaking alert before it is sent, and we recommend that an outside human expert reads the case first.
proofStandard.otherwise: Until a case passes, or if it fails, the level can't go above Warning, and the case is shown as under investigation (or failed) on this page.

caseFile.name: Alarm case-file standard
caseFile.note: The format of a Level-3 alarm, fixed before any case exists so that a case can't be shaped to fit a story. The breaking email and the case page follow it section by section, and a full evidence appendix is published on the site.
caseFile.verdict: One sentence, first: what we conclude, and why it meets the Level-3 standard.

sections.title: What we claim, and what we don't
sections.requires: The exact claim: which Level-3 trigger, which system and whose, since when, and what it does. Then, just as plainly, what we are not claiming.

sections.title: The independent lines of evidence
sections.requires: Each line, with every fact, its source and how it was authenticated, and the inference drawn from it. Then why the lines are independent: each line's original sources, none shared.

sections.title: Every innocent explanation we considered
sections.requires: Each innocent explanation, the defense's strongest version of it, and the evidence it fails to explain.

sections.title: What could have disproved it, and proof we checked
sections.requires: The findings that would have sunk the case, how we checked each one and what we found, with sources.

sections.title: What we still don't know
sections.requires: Open questions and the weakest links in the case.

sections.title: What readers can do
sections.requires: How to check the evidence yourself, how to send us evidence either way, and how to follow the case.

caseFile.correction: If the case turns out to be wrong, we publish a correction the same day, log it in the alarm history and the corrections log, and the level drops at once under the retraction rule.
caseFile.appendix: Every case gets a full evidence appendix page: each source with an archived copy, every authentication step, how the lines were kept independent, the defense's full case, and each judge's verdict and reasons.
caseFile.register: Every case, open, passed or failed, is listed in this file's cases list as {id, trigger, status, opened, decided, file, page}. A met Y trigger names its case in a case field, and counts only when that case has passed.

fields.lines: at least three: [{id, modality, summary, facts: [{fact, source, authentication, archive}], inference, originalSources: [...]}], each from a different modality, no original source shared
fields.independence: why no two lines share an original source
fields.tribunal: {prosecution, defense, authenticity: [{item, method, result}], judges: [{id, verdict: proven or not proven, reasons}], unanimous: true or false}

triggers.trigger: Capability gap between internal and public frontier models, measured or credibly reported
triggers.threshold: 3 months or more, measured by an evaluator (such as METR, or an AI Security Institute comparing internal and public models) or credibly reported (a lab's own statement, or reporting that meets the evidence standard). Our own estimate doesn't count.
triggers.why: About one frontier release cycle: long enough for a capability to go unseen for a full cycle.
triggers.clears: A newer measurement or credible report puts the gap under 3 months, or the internal models behind it are released.

triggers.trigger: A newly released or disclosed model far above the capability trend, implying hidden progress beforehand
triggers.threshold: A model released or disclosed in the past 90 days scores 3 or more residual standard deviations above the published frontier-trend fit for its release date, on an instrument that can measure that level: METR's time horizon while the threshold stays within METR's reliable range (16 hours today), or the Epoch Capabilities Index or METR's successor long-task suite once this site publishes a fit for it. If no instrument can measure it, X2 can't be observed, which isn't the same as not met.
triggers.why: Three residual SDs is far outside the normal scatter of frontier models around the trend: on METR's 50% horizon it is about 4x the trend value, or about 8.5 months ahead. A jump that size on release means the progress was made out of view.
triggers.clears: 90 days pass after the model's release or disclosure with no other model above the threshold, or sooner if the measurement is revised below it.
triggers.evidence: Can't be observed today. Both thresholds are above METR's 16-hour reliable range, and this site doesn't yet publish an Epoch Capabilities Index fit. changelog.change: Evidence and rationale corrections only: primary source for W5, corrected W4 rationale (SB 53 reports are confidential), published X6 ruling, borderline and observability flags, and W3 sourced to Politico and Bloomberg. No threshold, rule or level changed.

Exit rule made symmetric: a level drops after its rule has gone unsatisfied for 30 consecutive days, to the level the rules then give. W1 counts only a measured or credibly reported gap, not our estimate. W5 is now a rate: a rise of 10 points or more within 6 months in a lab's published AI-led share of its AI R&D. Borderline values don't count. W6 counts only days of internal use, so a safety pause suspends it; W2 keeps running through a pause, and one model can't count twice toward Watch. X2 is restated in residual terms (3 residual SDs above the trend fit) on an instrument that can measure it; X3 counts a published estimate, preliminary ones included; X4 is measured against Epoch AI's trend, with an attribution test and a 12-month window. Y1 names both halves of our strict bar. Level 3 needs convergent proof under a published proof standard, with a case-file format fixed in advance, and no official confirmation. Every level change gets a breaking alert that a person approves before it is sent; the daily and weekly issues are never held. Every trigger now says when it clears. Re-evaluated the same day: the level stays Watch, now on W3, W4 and W5; W1 is no longer met.
changelog.why: Under v1.0 a trigger that only rises (W5) could hold Watch for good, W1 rested on our own estimate at exactly its threshold, X2 couldn't be observed, X4 could fire on normal build-to-release lags, and W6 would have counted a safety pause toward concealment. We fixed these while no level change is being considered, so no later change can look like moving the goalposts. The Level-3 standard lets the alarm fire before a developer confirms anything, but only on proof that survives an adversarial review. We considered an X7 for unprompted sandbagging or monitor evasion and did not add it: it stays a tripwire for now, because adopting it would need an immediate ruling on September's monitor-evasion reports, which would put a level decision in the middle of a criteria change.
